## Quick Reader

### Symbols and notation

To keep the formulas uniform, this chapter uses the following notation.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $K$ | Laboratory or floor Cartesian frame with coordinates $\mathbf r=(X,Y,Z)$. |
| $\mathcal B$ | Reference base of the lattice, typically an interval for a transfer line or a closed path for a ring. |
| $s$ | Reference or reporting coordinate on $\mathcal B$; in an $s$-integrator it is also the independent variable. |
| $t$ | Physical time and the independent variable of the current OPALX tracker. |
| $U_i$, $u_i$ | Canonical local chart of element $i$ and the corresponding local coordinates. |
| $\psi_i:U_i\to\mathbb{R}^3$ | Intrinsic geometry map of element $i$ in its canonical frame. |
| $\Omega_i\subset U_i$ | Local support region on which the element field, aperture, or material model is defined. |
| $\Sigma_{i,\alpha}\subset\overline{U_i}$ | Marked geometric interface chart of element $i$; it need not lie on the boundary of the field support. |
| $p_{i,\alpha}=(\Sigma_{i,\alpha},F_{i,\alpha})$ | Port $\alpha$ of element $i$, consisting of a boundary chart together with an adapted frame $F_{i,\alpha}$. |
| $P_i(u_i,t)$ | Placement map that embeds the local chart of element $i$ into the laboratory frame. |
| $\mathcal S_i(t)=P_i(\Omega_i,t)$ | Placed support of element $i$ in laboratory space at time $t$. |
| $T_i(t)$ | Rigid placement transform of element $i$ at time $t$; it may be written as a rotation matrix $R_i(t)$ together with a translation vector $\mathbf a_i(t)$. |
| $\Gamma_i(\ell)$ | Optional local reference path of element $i$, parameterized by the local longitudinal coordinate $\ell\in[0,L_i]$. |
| $C_{pq}$ | Rigid transition or patch transform from port $p$ to port $q$. |
| $g_{ij}$ | Transition map between neighboring local charts. |

### A geometric viewpoint

Following Forest and Hirata [@foresthirata], one should distinguish the
placed physical object from the coordinates used to describe it. In that
spirit, an OPALX element is not first of all an interval in one global
coordinate $s$. It is a local chart $U_i$, an intrinsic geometry map
$\psi_i$, a support region $\Omega_i\subset U_i$, and a finite set of marked
interfaces through which that local chart is connected to neighboring charts.

In the proposed model, a port of element $i$ consists of a marked geometric
interface chart and an adapted frame:

$$\Sigma_{i,\alpha}\subset\overline{U_i},\qquad p_{i,\alpha}=(\Sigma_{i,\alpha},F_{i,\alpha}).$$

Examples are entrance, exit, branch, fiducial and ring-closure interfaces.
A body entrance or exit need not coincide with the boundary of the field
support $\Omega_i$, particularly when fringe fields extend beyond the body.
The advantage of introducing the word "port" is that the same notion works for
a straight drift, a curved bend, a patch, a branch, or a ring-closing
connection.

In the proposed representation, connecting two ports would store transition
data between their local descriptions. This is a chart-to-chart coordinate
change; the fibre-bundle interpretation relates local trivializations
[@foresthirata]. Ports organize that proposed connectivity without introducing
new physics. Current OPALX instead stores element transforms and ordered
sequence membership, without a general named-port connection object.

A transfer line is then an open chain of ports, while a ring is a closed
chain, possibly only up to a prescribed symmetry transform. That is the
geometric reason the same placement model can cover both linear and circular
machines.

### Why the independent variable matters

Comparisons with established accelerator codes provide a useful baseline:
MAD-X describes the machine primarily as an ordered sequence of elements
along a reference orbit, and survey or optics calculations are performed
relative to that backbone [@madxprimer; @madxptc]. The cited manuals illustrate different emphases in placement and modeling:
Elegant remains strongly sequence-centric, MARYLIE is more map-first, IMPACT-T
uses ordered field regions with local frame changes, and Bmad exposes geometry
operators such as patches and fiducials
[@elegantmanual; @marylie; @impactt; @bmad].

In an **$s$-based tracker**, longitudinal position along a reference curve
is the independent variable. Many lattice descriptions also use that
coordinate to order elements. This does not prevent three-dimensional survey
geometry, local coordinate changes, field overlap or branch connections.

In a **$t$-based tracker**, particles advance in physical time and may
simultaneously occupy different machine regions. Field evaluation therefore
needs the particle position and each element’s local frame and support.
OPALX combines time-based tracking with an ordered reference-coordinate
representation; compatible analytic rings also use spatial support selection.
Named ports are a proposed way to organize connectivity, not a requirement
imposed by choosing $t$ as the independent variable.

This leads to the main OPALX conclusion:

1. topology,
2. survey or reference-curve metadata,
3. rigid placement in laboratory space, and
4. physics field evaluation

should be treated as separate concepts, even if they are often conflated in
traditional $s$-based lattice descriptions.
